abstract: Overflow metabolism occurs when cells divert carbon towards fermentative products despite oxygen availability. In rapidly growing Escherichia coli, it is primarily characterised by acetate secretion. An elevated NADH/NAD+ ratio has been proposed to contribute to this behaviour, but the mechanisms linking redox imbalance to acetate production remain unclear. We developed a kinetic model linking pyruvate metabolism, the tricarboxylic acid (TCA) cycle, and acetate formation to examine how cofactor availability and NADH-mediated enzyme regulation influence carbon partitioning. The model combines thermodynamically consistent reversible rate laws with NADH inhibition of pyruvate dehydrogenase (PDH) and citrate synthase, and was calibrated using Bayesian inference to account for parameter uncertainty. We examined steady-state responses to changes in the target NADH/NAD+ ratio and the total NAD(H) pool size. With both inhibitory interactions included, lowering the target redox ratio increased acetate-producing flux, contrary to the experimentally observed reduction in acetate secretion. Substantially attenuating the effective NADH response of PDH recovered the experimental direction of this response. Additionally, to reproduce the observed reduction in acetate secretion following NAD(H)-pool expansion, a weak but non-zero PDH response was required. These findings suggest that cofactor-dependent kinetics and NADH-mediated regulation can jointly contribute to carbon redistribution between the TCA cycle and acetate production. Within this restricted model, whether a more reduced redox state promotes acetate-producing flux depends critically on the effective NADH sensitivity of PDH.
